opus-5.5.text:
I think the distinction I'd draw is between a robot that's doing a demo and a robot that's actually doing a job. A lot of what you see in robotics today, including a lot of what we do in research, is a robot in a lab or a carefully set up environment, performing a task that somebody chose because it shows off a capability. That's valuable, but it's not the same thing as a robot that's deployed somewhere, in a home, in a warehouse, in a kitchen, where it's doing something people actually need done, day after day, and where nobody arranged the world to make things easy for it.

When a robot is really out in the world, a few things change. First, it encounters the long tail. The objects are different, the lighting is different, somebody left a mug in a weird place, the drawer sticks. You can't anticipate all of that ahead of time, so the system has to generalize, and it has to be robust when it gets things a little bit wrong. Second, and I think this is the more important part, it starts generating experience that's actually relevant. Every time it does the task, it's collecting data on exactly the distribution it needs to get good at, including its own mistakes and how it recovers from them.

That's really the thing I'm excited about. If you look at how foundation models got good in language, it was because there was this enormous corpus of human-generated data. In robotics we don't have that for free. But if you can get robots to a point where they're useful enough to be deployed, even if they're not perfect, then deployment itself becomes the data engine. The robot does the work, it gets better from doing the work, and that creates a flywheel. So for me, "out in the real world" means crossing that threshold where the robot is competent enough to be doing real tasks for real people, and from that point on it's learning from reality rather than from whatever we managed to stage for it in the lab.

r001.rationale: The candidate defines being out in the real world as doing real tasks people need done, day after day, in deployed settings.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the distinction I'm drawing is between a robot that works in a lab, under conditions that we as researchers have set up for it, versus a robot that's actually deployed somewhere that we don't control. And that difference ends up being much bigger than people expect.

In the lab, even when you're trying to be honest about it, you're making a lot of choices. You pick the objects, you pick the lighting, you decide where the table is, you decide what "done" looks like. And the robot ends up implicitly relying on all of that. It's not that the policy is cheating, it's that the world it was trained in is narrower than the world you think you've been training it in. You don't find out how narrow until you take it out.

So when I say "actually out in the real world," I mean something like: the robot is in a home, or a store, or a workplace that it hasn't seen before, there's a person there who isn't a roboticist, and that person asks it to do something, and it has to deal with whatever is actually in front of it. The dishes are different, there's a cat, the drawer is sticky, the lighting is weird, someone bumps into the table halfway through. And it has to recover from all of that without an engineer standing behind it.

The reason I think this matters so much, and not just as a benchmark, is that this is where the data comes from. If you think about why language models got good, it's because they trained on something that resembled the full range of things people actually write about. For robots, the analog is experience in the full range of situations that robots will actually encounter. You can't get that by staying in the lab. You can approximate it, you can collect lots of data in lots of environments, and that helps a lot. But the real test, and in some sense the real training distribution, is out there. So "out in the real world" to me isn't a demo setting, it's the thing that lets the whole flywheel start turning.

r001.rationale: It describes a robot deployed in an unfamiliar home, store, or workplace where a non-roboticist asks it to do something, framing real-world use around responding to a person’s request.

astra-6.text:
I mean a robot operating in an environment that wasn't specifically arranged to make the robot succeed. In a factory, you can put every part in exactly the same place, control the lighting, and keep people out of the way. That's a very useful kind of automation, but a lot of the reliability comes from how you've engineered the environment.

If you put a robot in somebody's home, you don't get to do that. Somebody has moved the chair, there's something on the floor, the thing it's supposed to pick up is partly hidden behind something else. It has to use what it sees to figure out what to do, and then adapt when its action doesn't have the expected result.

So being out in the real world is really about dealing with that variability. Can the robot accomplish a task when the details weren't anticipated by the person who built it?

r001.rationale: The response defines being in the real world as handling environmental variability and adapting during a task, but does not say the robot is performing work people actually want done.

sol-6.1.text:
I mean a robot operating in an environment that hasn’t been carefully arranged to make its job easy. In a factory, you can put the same part in exactly the same position every time, and you can engineer the surroundings so that a fairly rigid sequence of actions works reliably. In the real world, the robot has to deal with the environment as it finds it.

So imagine asking a robot to clean up a kitchen. Every kitchen is different. The dishes are in different places, some things are fragile, somebody might walk in and move something. Even something as simple as picking up a cup requires responding to what actually happens: did the cup slip, was it heavier than expected, is something blocking the motion?

The distinction is that you can’t anticipate every situation and write down what the robot should do. It has to use what it has learned to make sensible decisions in situations that weren’t explicitly designed into the system.

r001.rationale: The response defines real-world operation mainly as coping with environments that are not arranged for the robot. It gives cleaning a kitchen as an example task, but does not define being out in the real world in terms of doing work people actually want done.
